blurb: This was not the comedic pick-me-up I had hoped for. I'm on an unintentional depressing film streak here, help!
It’s brilliant but the vibes were so unexpectedly dark. It reads a bit like horror to me.

I saw the 35mm print at the Heights Theater with Jenny and Joey. Lovely time. But I had forgotten how much this film is incredibly enjoyable and also impossibly difficult to watch. Buckle up for that third act.

I don’t think this is for everyone, but it’s definitely for me. This got me very jazzed to see the new print of The Devils. (and I might have looked up some beginner tap dancing tutorials in an awkward fog of inspiration)

I learned that this was another film that the execs cut to pieces, which was arguably what undermined its box office numbers. For his part, Russell also refused to promote the edited version. 

It’s strange to discover these masterpieces now, knowing they were never properly distributed in their own time.
It’s a worthier sequel than Bride of Frankenstein, but the plot felt a bit overwrought at times. Still, Cushing carried the show and left me wanting more from the Hammer series.

It’s incredible what Raimi, Tapert, and Campbell achieved on such a minuscule budget. This time it was the sound design and foley that stood out most to me: the varied demonic vocalizations, a grandfather clock chiming through cavernous reverb, the driving, accelerating howl of pursuing evil (heard in the several first person shots and at one point depicted emanating from a deadite’s glassy eyes!). 

Rewatching this for the first time since I was in high school, it was just as much the gory, spooky thrill ride that I remember. The movie feels old as heck but it’s aged very well.
Stuart Gordon and Brian Yuzna are true masters of a certain flavor of B horror filth that you simply CANNOT recommend to others. Please don’t see this on my account!

A complete makeover of Mary Shelley, but I love it. The opening graveyard scene alone is sweet perfection to me. The atmospheric staging, lighting, and impeccable performances by Colin Clive (Frankenstein) and Dwight Frye (Fritz) gave me chills. Karloff is a wild lumbering force of nature, but I’m mostly here for that initial duo.

Other performances fall pretty flat: particularly those of the actors playing Elizabeth and Victor. Whale didn’t care anywhere near as much about those characters and it shows. 

When this film is at its best the camera is at a distance, drinking in the arresting, elaborate sets (holy laboratory!) and letting the actors do their magnificent work in long single takes. The conversation montage in contrast is a joke. These talkies clearly had no idea what they were doing yet! 

So it’s an uneven masterpiece, arguably an affront to Shelley, but man when Frankenstein cooks, it COOKS.

I don’t understand why some prefer this to the first. Yes it has a real, engaging score and that was majorly missing in the original. And yes many of the secondary characters are performed by competent film actors now. But if you ask me, the comedic antics and silly plot moves spoil the unique electricity the first installment had. 

No spoilers, but there is some outstanding movie magic nestled into this. Quite impressive for its time. And Karloff is still Karloff. No notes really. I can’t tell you much about the bride, because she’s only on screen for maybe 5 mins! Lol what? Truth in advertising, guys!! 

On a closing note: if the first was a bit disrespectful to the legacy of Mary Shelley, this one digs up her corpse and stiches together a mockery from its pieces. The opening scene depicting the original literary crew in particular is egregious. But eh, I found the book to be a depressing slog, so I’m not going to cry about it (no tears left after said slog!). 

The original film is the place to go if you want that classic Universal monster mayhem. This one might have attracted fans at the time, but it pales in comparison: especially if you see them back to back like I did.
This is really really bad. But also kind of ok for riffing on.

While Mary Shelley’s scientist was tragic, Universal’s was mad. But Hammer gives us an evil scientist à la Peter Cushing and man does it work for me. It’s no wonder this was Hammer’s major breakthrough into horror.
It's frivolous, spooky fun, with some very charming stagecraft. The story and characters are quite dated, in good and bad ways.
This had me at its ridiculous trailer. My expectations going in were a bit low, but it delivered some excellent Hammer-meets-Hitchcock atmosphere and suspense.

As much as I love older horror films, they rarely send true shivers down my spine like the best modern horror does. The Exorcist is a wild exception. 

First, it does a fantastic job of developing the bleak back stories of its core characters. And I love how they chose to make the mother a bit of a prick instead of the usual mom-as-saint cliche. By the time the nightmare starts to build, you have a good, clear sense of the personal stakes. 

And that nightmare is vivid and ferocious. The practical effects here are totally engrossing; there's really nothing you could do with modern effects to improve on them. What a ride!
I have this terrible hereditary condition where I have to watch every new Evil Dead movie that comes out. This is probably the worst in the series, but it wasn’t terrible.

I loved the other worldly style here. It had plenty of warts (nudge) but also tons of variety to offer. Movie magic for days. Every tenth scene or so was one of the coolest horror sequences I've seen. Evil Dead meets Sailor Moon?

I didn’t like this as much on our second viewing. The story has great bones, and several scenes really rip, but a lot of the film is weighed down by Flanagan’s sentimentality, which didn’t work for me here. 

And the callbacks to the Shining get pretty tiresome. I hadn’t seen the Shining recently when I first saw Doctor Sleep so I didn’t pick up on as much of the fan service. Seeing them back to back makes this installment lose a bit of its shine.

Saw this on 35mm at the heights with Jenny, Andrew, Annie, and Joey. Excellent pacing, cinematography, acting. Though the rewatch made me question Jack Nicholson's performance a bit. The character is iconic, no doubt, but Nicholson hams it up a bit too much imo. 

And I wish he could have taken some of the family drama bits more seriously. There's no real chemistry between Jack and Wendy or Danny at the start, which takes some of the gravity out of the rapid decline depicted in the rest of the film. 

Still, it's a masterpiece. One of the greatest horror films of its era.

It had some solidly spooky scenes and interesting proto-Giallo elements in the first of the three tales. But it was Boris Karloff’s send off at the end that made it all worth while for me. Pitch perfect horror hosting there.
Far from the best of Hammer horror, but still good fun. The story teaches us the unspeakable consequences of casting Peter Cushing as a villain.
It's Poe with shorter sentences. The more reasonably developed story is welcome, but the cheap set design, weird acting, and awkward plot kills it.

Pairing up a 20 year old Jamie Lee with a thoroughly grizzled Tom Atkins at 44 was a choice.

Overall this was fun if uneven. I dug the haunted atmosphere, Carpenter’s score, and most of the acting, though I thought the few key horror sequences mostly fell flat. Side note: Widow’s Bay apparently owes a lot to this weird old flick.
Vincent Price sure does a convincing evil incarnate.

Another Lynch film that I saw as part of the Heights Theater’s “Moving Through Time” series with Joey. Another impeccably morbid experience. 

I was able to relate a bit more with the protagonist here, and that helped me have more weird fun with this crime thriller/strange comedy.

I saw this troubling take on parenthood at the Heights Theater with Joey as part of their ongoing series on Lynch. I admire Lynch’s craftsmanship. Eraserhead looks and sounds incredible, and his otherworldly style is remarkably cohesive. 

I often like to dig into the meaning and/or guiding concept behind avant-garde films, but I think Lynch makes it clear in interviews that this is the wrong way to approach his films. This is one of the main reasons I find him so challenging. Side note: assuming I get his drift, I think he’s pretty funny in interviews.
This was much more absurd than I was expecting, but it also had some sweet, insightful moments that'll stick with me. Heads up: lots of alcohol drinking ahead.

Don Bluth is essentially Todd Solondz for kids. Does every scene need to menace me so much? That said, I love that our hero is a single mother. Walt would have had her ritually sacrificed in the opening scene. 

The voice acting, animation, and story are all excellent here. However, the music/score is very hit or miss. Also, Don is right about cats: they’re an invasive disaster for native wildlife when allowed outdoors.

I really wanted to like this more than I did. It had some incredible scenes, and the practical effects really worked at several points. The script had high and low points; but the third act kind of killed it for me.

It sometimes felt like it had an inflated sense of itself, but I did enjoy parts of this. I think much of my enjoyment came from appreciating it as a reimaging of Sartre's No Exit. It doesn't add any depth to the play, but it's a fun ride and I spent a lot of time thinking about the existentialist themes in its source material. 

No Exit really centers on a round robin series of rocky conservations between the characters, and when It Ends is at its best, it's following that formula.

I saw this with Joey and Greg at a series called Strange Hours hosted by the Heights Theater. It has a great heart and sense of purpose imo. 

The use of the "Eton Boating Song" in the start and end credits is perfect. While a lot of people go just for the final act, I actually think it's a tad overrated. The slow burn build in the first two acts is what does it for me.
This is one of the best modern horror movies I've seen. The performances are just incredible. I'm really excited to see what Curry Barker does next.

I didn't really care for this, despite being by Billy Wilder who I usually love. I thought the politics were really clumsy and dated. It had some of the pizazz of a good Billy Wilder movie, but without the plot to back it up.
The premise, directing, and FOLEY are out of this world. This is a perfect horror film for me.
